english: In the new covenant, the testimonies taken from the book of the Psalms are set forth as having been spoken by the Holy Spirit. Paul, having taken a chapter from the ninety-fourth Psalm in the epistle to the Hebrews, writes that it was announced by the Holy Spirit, saying, 'As the Holy Spirit says: If today you hear his voice...' (Hebrews 3:7), and the following. To this, Peter, the forerunner of the apostles, also says in the Acts of the apostles according to the pattern: 'It was necessary for the scripture to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who seize Jesus' (Acts 1:16), and the following, having said a few words, he brought forward: 'For it is written in the book of Psalms: Let his habitation become a desert, and let him not dwell in it; and let another take his oversight' (Psalm 69:25). It is nothing foreign if the apostles write these things, especially since the Savior is sealing these things. For a memory having occurred in the Gospel of the ninety-first Psalm at the beginning, sounding thus: 'The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet' (Psalm 109:1), the Pharisees were eager to ask if David, in the Holy Spirit, says Christ is Lord, how he is his son. If, therefore, the Psalms contain spiritual meanings, it was not by chance that they were composed in their scripture.

2 Ps 1,1 It is the way of sinners for the devil to say, in which the one having become [one] should not remain, following the deceptive teaching: 'Resist the devil and he will flee from you' (James 4:7). He who does not stand in this way will come to the one saying, 'I am the way' (John 14:6), and if, having become [one], running according to the purpose, he will win the prize. 3 Ps 1,3 ab For how must the one testified to by the things said, as being wise, not resemble wisdom? For someone resembles one bestowing such a quality, or does not the righteous resemble the just...

Eternal and holy in holiness; if this is so, then the wise man is also wise in wisdom. Having approached and broken being away from it, the wise man becomes like it, according to what was said by the Savior: 'It is sufficient for the disciple that he become as his teacher, and the servant as his lord' (Matt 10:25).

And he who becomes like the tree of life is planted in paradise to be with it; thus it is heard of what is written in Isaiah from the face of God: 'The days of the people of my God shall be as the days of the wood of life' (Isa 66:19). This being true, since the wood of life is eternal, it joins and shares in the passion of Him; thus the likeness makes us grow together in the wood, so that we may be made branches and shoots to bring forth divine fruit. For the wood of life is said to be a true vine toward those becoming imitators through goodness: 'I am the true vine; you are the branches; my Father is the gardener; every branch abiding in me, he prunes it, so that it may bear more fruit' (John 15:1, 2, 5).

But also, the mystical and spiritual understanding of the Scriptures is a fruit of the wood planted by the watercourses (this is the wisdom of God), and the ready words are leaves covering the said fruit, intended to do the proper work in guarding the fruits and becoming food for the most pure men, those called simple like cattle, according to: 'You will save men and cattle, Lord' (Ps 35:6).

For if they desire to be in the deficiency of dust through impiety and to bear the image of the swine, similarly they are swept away from the face of the earth by the most meager dust, being scattered there by the evil wind. english: By the guile of men in cunning. 6 Ps 1:5 The ungodly shall rise, but they shall not be judged, being self-condemned for being. For he who does not believe in me, he says, is already judged, having been shown to be condemned from his own unbelief. Ps 1:6a The deeds of the righteous are owned by God; for by this He knows them here. 7 Ps 1:6b Having been shown that the ungodly are not raised in judgment, it has been revealed how many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth are raised, some to eternal life, and others to eternal reproach and shame. For how is it that those being raised to be judged do not rise to eternal reproach and shame, the judgment itself making their sins manifest? If indeed this has become clear, why is it not said that all those sleeping in the dust of the earth are raised, some to eternal life, and others to eternal reproach and shame? For these things have been written concerning only those sinners coming unto judgment and the righteous being raised unto eternal life; of the ungodly, there is nothing of these being raised, nor will there be an examination of them after the resurrection. 8 Ps 2:8 Of all men moving by choice (for they are free agents), no one is essentially good or bad; and since the one possessing virtue is owned by God alone, and every such one becomes an inheritance of God. The whole of Israel was not good; it was said concerning him, 'He became a portion of the Lord, a branch of the inheritance of Israel Jacob.' It is shown that this nation did not only become an inheritance, but through goodness was so treated from what is said concerning God by the holy men: 'He chose for us His inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom He loved.' If, however, one keeps the commandments and the faith toward God, one becomes an inheritance of God; the one transgressing the commandments of God and falling away from faith toward Him is cast out from such honor, just as he who turns from evil and does good becomes a lot of God even if he was not so before. This sequence remaining, he who formerly through godliness was an heir of God, Israel, becoming an apostate of God, fell away, not receiving the one who previously went before him in blessing, even as also for all other men, the Savior has come. It is necessary, therefore, that another, being fulfilled from many nations, should be brought in and approach...

It is said regarding the gospel: 'You will not add to me, and I will give you life instead of death' (cf. John 10:28), but it is not said of the Son; for it shows that he adds nothing to himself, but rather to those who are in need; just as to a physician and teacher things are given, so that they may become healthy and knowledgeable from him.

But also the saying 'The ends of the earth shall hold fast to you' is understood more simply: until the ends of the earth, his teaching shall prevail, the gospel being preached in all creation under the heaven. If it is possible for the ends of the earth to be called here, understand those who have passed through the earth in life and wisdom.

Ps 2:10: 'Now receive understanding, you risen from the dead who were crucified; and you, rulers, be instructed, knowing what you honored by surrounding with death, having risen, having loosed death' (Ps 2:9 allusion); for this will turn you to serve in fear, knowing what is being plotted against you, what God is, through which you have come. This slavery in fear will cease, having produced progress, so that divine exultation may come to you with trembling; for if any joy comes reasonably, it is exultation; but it does not happen before God with mere trembling. With this, 'Shout for joy to God with a voice of exultation, who is the Most High and awesome' (Ps 2:11 allusion) is consistent; for since the exultation is of the Most High and awesome, it is necessary to have it with trembling.

Ps 2:12a–c: The saying 'Seize instruction' is spoken in an extraordinary way, as if to be the follower of the phrase: 'Seize instruction quickly, and what you are encountering in this life, lest, while you are being sluggish, the Lord be angry and you perish from the way of righteousness' (Ps 2:12).

Ps 3:4: Since it was said that the psalm is proclaimed before the face of the Lord (Ps 3:4), it must be said that his head is also raised, the God who is, or that his divinity becomes manifest to the faithful through demonstration. The contemplative. Since now David perceives God and His truth with a pure heart, he utters a song, and he says that things are in the psalms because he has achieved much in a practical way. This song is that which they are accustomed to call the end, the most desired of his own things, while all other things are to be chosen and desired, but not for the sake of another; for it is the perfection of all things, concerning which also Paul says, 'If one has become like God, he will see Him' (1 John 3:2).

What, then, does the author intend by saying the song is for David but not written by David? Some say, then, that the psalm or the song belongs to David, but that he himself, having been inspired by God, brought it forward, while the song or the psalm belongs to David, but the things said have a reference to him. And often what is announced belongs both to him and to him; either that which is being suggested was foretold by him through his ministry of the Spirit, or that the psalm being given to someone who sings was announced to David through them. Whichever it may be of those written in the Scriptures, it is known only to the one who is wise according to God.

Having received this word, the apostle brought it to it: 'Let not the sun go down on your anger, nor give place to the devil' (Ephesians 4:26). He who has received this apostolic exhortation, being angry, does not sin by persisting in staying angry and calling it monthly anger. This thought is confirmed by what follows: 'For you say' (clearly being angry) 'in your hearts, strike upon your beds, so as to have risen from sleep and to have done or said nothing of those in the heart covered in anger' (Psalm 4:4).

It is possible to call the Light of the face of God the character of the substance and the icon of the invisible God, through which light it was signaled toward us, having been formed according to Him (Psalm 4:6). It should not be ignored how some read 'Who will show us the good things thus'; the good things are not of many, but it is of one to show; and he is the only-begotten Son of God. By 'thus' they take 'Who' as signifying specifically what is unique and one in number in essence. It is conjoined with the witness 'A certain noble man', for there the 'Who' signifies what is uniquely such.

Even if you do not receive glory from the pleasures of yourselves, but I, expecting an age to come and the reward of upright citizenship, having become free from all disturbance through hope, 'I will sleep and lie down also' (Psalm 4:8), saying the departure from life; giving the reason for having slept and having slumbered in peace, he immediately brought to it 'You have settled me on hope' (Psalm 4:9). It is also said in the Psalms toward the soul from the face of God, 'I will dwell in hope'. God does this, proposing the hope of coming divine good things to those dwelling by Him in intellectual and practical virtue and in doctrines of truth and ecclesiastical laws.

He prays for the soul being brought forward, that the church might be prepared for a divine inheritance for those who are healers of God; for inheritance belongs to those being healed by the Lord. But this inheritance is not corruptible and does not possess being in sensible wealth; for it is said that the heirs of this are to be brought into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, kept in the heavens (1 Peter 1:4). Into this, the Savior calls the worthy: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you' (Matthew 25:34). Having received this, the one speaking the present psalm says he is sending a prayer to the one who has made it favorable to God, that he might be worthy to be shown an heir of it according to the New Covenant, just as he signifies concerning his own soul by the inscription 'For the one inheriting.'

As for 'To enlighten,' it is not used in a common way; in the Scripture, it constantly signifies receiving into the ears the words being announced by the speaker because of their nearness. It is said that the righteous are near to God, that God hearkens to the prayers of the righteous and has them in his heed for their supplication (Psalm 5:2-3). And God turns out to be a King and Creator of those who have not stretched out their hands toward a foreign god, nor are they ruled by sin.

According to theory, then: to whom the sun of righteousness has risen, having come into being at the beginning of an intelligible day, bringing a gift of grace to the cause of illumination. 'In the morning,' he says, 'hearkening to my voice' (Psalm 30:4); for to whom must one confess such a great good, O Lord, regarding the one who caused light to rise for me, existing as the greatest vision? For he always enters into the visions that are to be and desires to see the beauties of the truth. This is also presented from the 'And I shall see.' For just as 'I am coming' signifies unceasing approach, so 'I shall see' manifests an ever-increasing comprehension; for how can he who has obtained the promise not always see, 'The Lord shall be your eternal light, and Light to the righteous always' (Isaiah 60:19; Malachi 4:2)? And there is another scripture possessing 'I shall present to you and you shall see me,' which does not speak of all, but of those speaking with boldness according to the great Elijah because of their departure from the polity.

english: The Lord presented him before him today (Ps 5:5–7). Since this is true, evil is not from God, unlike those who make evil their very substance. For from the mouth of the Most High, evil shall not come out, nor the good [alone]. For He alone wills the good to be; it is impossible for evil to exist in any way.

And those who speak falsehood are lying, so that they might know the truth which they formerly feared. For knowing this is evident: no one, having begun to know something, is said to be 'knowing' it [unless he has mastered it]. And of all those speaking falsehood who are being destroyed by God, that one also shall be destroyed, as it is said: 'Whoever speaks falsehood, speaks from his own [nature].' If this is so, he is not evil in essence; for it is not merely by becoming and entering into a substance, but after this, having turned to the habit of speaking falsehood, having once had the truth to be. This is shown by what is written about him: 'He has not stood in the truth, there is no truth in him' (Ps 51:7). For the liar, because he does not stand [in truth], is manifest having been tested by these dispositions.

One must judge the liar by his intention, but not by voice alone, lest those who once acted providentially like Rahab be under the threat; for it seemed to be lying to those searching to kill the spies, who were good men; but having been sent by Joshua son of Nun, they were praised. Since the intention of a man is very important, it is not appropriate to rank it among the being destroyed or among those speaking falsehood. Just as he who kills a man in a certain way is not a murderer, so likewise he who sheds blood is not always a man [of that name]; for we do not say 'murderers of blood' of men who kill according to divine law those worthy to suffer this, since it is said of Samuel and Elijah, the great men, having been testified to regarding ag...

It is not to lie in unholiness and divine prophecy to be subject to these crimes, but none of these is a murderer or a man of blood, even if he kills someone on account of impiety and greatest crimes. When these are rightly confessed, the man who becomes the cause of the abolition of the law through transgression is to be called a murderer and a man of blood. And the deceitful is reasonably joined to this; for how is he who pours out the blood of men treacherously not loathsome to the Lord?

It must be examined how anyone is led by the justice of God. Lest perhaps he who progresses according to the justice of God (for that is genuine virtue) following God, 'Afterwards you shall walk, Lord, my God' (Ps 5:11), is led by the one who provides virtue, namely, God himself. And since the 'offending' is human, it must be observed how it is necessary to take what is said about God. God, being unchangeable and immutable, is impassible, though it seems he is surrounded by passions or we experience passions; for our passions, being considered as approaching Him, because of the forgetfulness we have concerning Him, are assumed to be His. Regarding us, indeed, 'Forget the law of your God, and I will forget you, my children' (Ps 5:12).

What is written by Paul is similar to this word: 'If anyone does not know, he is not known' (1 Cor 13:12); it is clear what is meant by the one speaking to the wicked, 'Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). Thus, he who offends, suffering what is worthy of his character through the most bitter wickedness, which he has done, thinks that God is offended against him. If, indeed, the soul, falling unjustly by the vote of God because of sins, says, 'I, offending, was offended' (Ps 5:5), and thus follows the sequence of the judgment, 'The Lord is just' (Ps 5:6), what did his mouth offend? All who hope in you will rejoice, those whose plots against them are destroyed. And there is joy for those who hope in you (Ps 5:11).

english: It is not short-lived nor temporary; rather, they will rejoice forever, because God dwells in them. For how could they not always rejoice when God is present, tabernacling as if in his own temple? For how could those who have God in themselves, dwelling and walking about, be near to joy, when the distance from God, caused by sin capturing them, is near to wails and lamentations?

The preceding words shall be said concerning the arrival of the Savior, the joy of all those waiting for his human appearance (Ps 5:12ab); for the prophets and those who understand the prophecies hoped for this. For the Word of God arrived having become flesh to dwell in those believing in him; for he says, 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14). Thus, having dwelt, those who received him in themselves will rejoice forever; for they see the glory of the Word having tabernacled among them through the flesh, as the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth; those of this time, rejoicing forever, having seen by work the glory of the one as the only-begotten from the Father, say: 'Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we no longer know him, having the vision of his glory as the only-begotten from the Father' (2 Cor 5:16).
The cross is both a weapon and a crown; a weapon for those warring, a crown for those conquering. And again: a weapon for the soldiers, a crown for those reigning.

But he is contained in hymns having a more divine thought, and he himself is such; and he also sees toward the end the most perfect things regarding the eighth. It must be considered what the spiritual circumcision is, which one having God is circumcised, not necessarily one being circumcised according to the flesh. For the prophet says to those striving only according to the flesh: 'Be circumcised to your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your uncircumcision' (Rom 2:29); and the same prophet says: 'All Gentiles are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts' (Rom 2:25). Therefore, he who is sensibly circumcised removes something of that which serves the generation of the member, just as he who casting out every thought friendly to the generation of the intellect circumcises the heart. This circumcision they have, the truly [believing]...

Those devoted to the things of the Lord, so as to please Him. For circumcision is established on the eighth day; for the circumcised must overcome the world that was created in six days, and this is to become on the seventh day a true, holy, and sweet Sabbath. And since the ceasing from worldly things is not sufficient for perfect blessedness, it is necessary to receive, after the Sabbath, a super-cosmic state as the eighth. He who has been tempted by this desire will not love the world nor the things in it. Toward this spiritual understanding he leads us, and the mixture with the command of the sensible circumcision does not save the Logos if it remains merely in bare histories: 'Every male shall be circumcised on the eighth day' (Exodus 12:48), he says. Regarding the transgression of what was commanded, a threat of destruction is set against the child not circumcised on the eighth day, but not against the parents or the one raising the child otherwise; for the threat seemed to be reasonable, if it were brought upon one of these, not saving the follower of the eight-day child from doing it, and especially the intention to keep the commandment of God.

He is reproved in anger, and his sins are not made manifest (Ps 6:2); being led by Him according to a bitter and painful guidance, just as one who has fallen under the wraths of God, receiving the sensation of the cause of the evil having happened, is being disciplined in anger for suffering these things. By this thought is said, regarding the wrath led toward the senses: 'I will endure the wrath of the Lord until I do wrong to Him,' so as not to justify my judgment and to turn away my judgment and to drive me into the light. For if one, having been led into such a state, knows that the wrath has been brought upon him from God by a way of healing, he will not at all be unwilling to be subject to it, so that the judgment might be justified on account of Him who judges not thus. For not he who, having endured the wrath according to the purpose of the one who led him, will be driven into the light by God, having turned away the judgment from Him. If, therefore, of those being reproved and being disciplined, some are so through anger and wrath, and others through logical teaching, these things are to be completed, and through toil they come to reproof and discipline. Those who imply that the upcoming words refer to common death err, but rather they act impiously. For the holy men do not have remembrance of God and the common life only then, but much more so, as they are separated from the corruptible body.

What do you say? Since no one, having remembered you, becomes in death—for sin does not die (and he is not the one separating the sinning soul from a virtuous life)—but I desire to have remembrance of you; for this purpose, having flowed out your goodness: save me, so that I may not be overcome by the weakness and trouble that is present against me, and be crushed by death. For it is not said, 'He does not remember God in death' (Ps 6:5), but rather, 'He who remembers him is not in death,' as the Savior says, 'He who hears my word does not see death for eternity' (John 8:51).

Look if it is possible to be made new against all my enemies (Ps 6:8) and to have another mind. He who lives with righteousness, always living in renewal according to the newness of the spirit and the new covenant; because, having departed from the praiseworthy life through our inattention, having become old according to the antiquity of that man, whom Paul advises to strip off (for his life is vain), that we may put on the new man created according to God in holiness and knowledge of the truth (Eph 4:22-24); such is the unblemished life.

You will understand that these things are said also regarding the invisible enemies and evil powers who have prepared a device against him, who are envious of his progress according to God, and who, after sin, speak wickedly, 'There is no salvation for him in his God' (Ps 6:10).

english: He will cease to act in such a way. The interpretation is confirmed by the approaching verse: 'the enemies, having been turned, no longer driving forward toward evil, but turning back into the virtuous life they left behind.' This happens to them for a good purpose, not by chronological succession or slowly, but let it happen very quickly.

Psalm 7:1: 'The son of Jemini was called from the people' (Ps 7:1), who was Saul, and Shimei, who denounced the message to Saul, a son of Arahi from his father, and the high priest was the leader of the friends and an old man according to friendship. He sings the psalm practically, while also bringing it forth theoretically. It is said in the inscription of the fourth that the psalm denotes practice, while the ode denotes theory; and since there are inscriptions having 'Psalm of an Ode' or 'Ode of a Psalm,' it must be said about them that Psalm 8 is a theory concerning practical and moral instruction, while Ode is the practice necessary to be received in contemplating the truth; for many things are done for the sake of the theory of wisdom, and no one will say a 'Psalm of an Ode' without purpose. These things being observed as an ode, it is fitting that David sings the present psalm practically while contemplating theoretically concerning each of the things being done wisely and very Godward, desiring to know what is signified by those things being accomplished in such a sensory way. And the words of the psalm beginning in such a way must also be set forth: 'Lord my God, etc.'

Psalm 7:2-3: 'Who is it that said, Saving is not from me, he who has come to seek and to save the lost, and to give his soul as a ransom for many?' (Ps 7:2-3). These signify that the Father God saves through the Son, the existing Word of God; therefore, even in the present matters, the divinity of Father and Son must not be divided, as some might suppose.

Psalm 7:7-8: 'I beseech you, Lord, arising in wrath, appear high at the ends of the enemies; for the end of iniquity will consume those things through which my enemies occur.' (Ps 7:7-8). It is possible to say the ends of the enemies are their arrogance and pride, upon which they have reached and consider themselves to be secure, thinking themselves to be in the best states. The prayer is not defensive; for he does not give back evil for evil.

When God, sparing the enemies who oppose Him, wishes them to know how God is exalted in their borders, He uses wrath not against their essence, but against the malicious intention they possess. Since the Scripture says, 'In the borders of my enemies,' it is revealed that those enemies are the enemies of the Holy and God. Psalm 7:9: 'Bring Your judgment upon me only according to Your wickedness and my righteousness; for I shall be justified when no iniquity is found in my deeds.' Regarding 'wickedness' here, he says, one must not lack goodness according to what is written, 'The innocent believes all words,' but rather the simplicity that cleanses from deceit, as signified by what is said to God by the Holy One: 'But I have taken hold of you through innocence,' and 'In innocence I have gone forward.' In certain copies, 'Judge me, Lord, according to Your righteousness,' the word is to be explained thus: there is a righteousness of God reaching to men, being distributed toward a lower righteousness.

Paul, writing about the difference of these things concerning the Jews, says, 'For I testify to them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for knowing not the righteousness of God, but seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God' (Romans 10:2-3). By saying the righteousness of God, he means that which comes to all who believe through Jesus Christ, which He Himself also desired. He says all things were sent so that one might be found having the righteousness from God through faith and not his own. Wishing this to be present also for the disciples, Jesus says to them, 'If your righteousness does not exceed that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5:20). This distinction between human righteousness and that of God, according to the will of the Lord, is to be judged, knowing how this judgment will lead Him to salvation.

english: They are called bodily. This is shown from many scriptures, one of which is: 'Near is their mouth, but far from their kidneys.' This is said concerning wicked men, who indeed confess that God exists by word, but do not have Him in their intellect. 'My help is just from God, who saves those upright in heart.' This teaches by power whether He saves those upright in heart. And I demand just help from Him, by which I shall be saved; that I may have an upright heart, free from all deceit; therefore I also pray to be judged according to my goodness (Ps 7:12–14).

Having brought a prayer so that the wickedness of sinners might be completed and the Lord might be exalted over the edges of the enemies, rising in wrath through love toward neighbors, He does not want anyone to suffer the completion of wickedness by chance, but to know it by choice, knowing God to be a judge. If God is a just judge, it is to be feared to sin; for we approach the Word as a judge seeing the hidden and not being ignorant of anything being done. And just as a judge, so also He is just, bringing the judgment according to merit to those judged under Him. And a judge who is just and has power can without delay punish those stumbling.

If no one receives justice from the ungodly and sinning ones, through the long-suffering of the judge's goodness, there is an overcoming of the retribution; for if a just and powerful judge were only [that], all would have been lost immediately, because the intellect of men is flowing toward sin, whereas He has [power] toward the things said and toward long-suffering. For He is good and does not bring wrath every single day, even though ungodliness and sins are happening constantly. But let us long-suffer not that we should persist in evil, but that we may have time and place for repentance; for He desires the repentance of the sinner so that he may live, rather than accepting death by persisting.

Regarding sinning, what is called being ignorant of what is the good of God for your repentance. However, even if he does not bring wrath on each day through exceeding goodness and patience, for those remaining in wickedness, wrath will be brought upon them in a day of wrath, that is, in a day of judgment. For if you do not turn back, he says, enjoying remaining in sin, he will make his sword shine (instead of being blunt).

And with it also his bow he will make ready, preparing in it instruments of death, having worked out the arrows of the punishments against those being burned from the fire of the sufferings. Often of the divine disciplines, the punishment is found being made manifest by the name of the sword. For that which is in Amos the prophet, 'All the sinners of the people shall be finished with the sword' (Amos 9:7), does not signify a physical knife; for not from everyone are all sinners slain by a hand-slaughter understood. It is not necessary that all the sinners be presented to be finished by punishment, being handed over to perish in Gehenna in soul and body.

The same is made manifest also in the prophet Zephaniah, saying of God: 'And you also, Ethiopians, are wounded by my sword' (Zephaniah 3:8), by which the sword of God is made clear, all the Ethiopian being called out through darkness and wickedness. Most clearly in Exodus, instead of a most bitter punishment, the sword was received; where the scribes of the sons of Israel, those over the works of the tyrant, having been appointed by him, having fallen under most bitter threat and tribulation, meeting Moses and Aaron, were saying, inciting: 'See, God has seen you and will judge; for you have made our stench loathsome before Pharaoh, to give the sword into his hands to kill us.' For they did not say they feared the iron knife, but the bitterness of the ruler, they said this. english: A sword, but it is shining. And the bow has been drawn and prepared to shoot the arrows of punishment, but it has not yet released the arrows, even though it has fashioned them and holds them ready to shoot. It can be said that instruments of death are prepared in a bow, those serving the punishments, often called instruments of wrath. For the wicked are not angels through whom wrath, anger, and tribulation are sent upon the worthy. And if even the fashioned arrows, having been filled with poisonous medicine, are instruments of death for those being punished, one must take heed.

He who has labored in iniquity has conceived pain to give birth to injustice (Ps 7:15–17). These are the offspring that the one who has conceived will bring forth in secret, he who is to be punished through iniquity and injustice which he did; and appropriately, he will seize both the pain in the punishment and the pain in the sinning. For the work of iniquity is most heavy and burdensome, compared to a talent of lead; for nothing is more inferior than evil, which always brings down the one who does it.

Some say that, because of the order of evil, the labor is spoken of before the seizing of the birth-pangs. For upon those pregnant, after the seizing, is the pain with which they give birth; but there, before the seizing, the pain is named because it lacks the rhythm and order of that in evil. And likewise the precedence of injustice over iniquity. For someone having become lawless from this, is not under the law of righteousness, so as to also set upon other men while he acts unjustly. This is found especially concerning Cain; for having become lawless by not rightly dividing what is due to God, he subsequently gave birth to injustice by attacking his brother lethally. Moreover, these voices belong especially to the devil, who is primeval-evil because he first acted lawlessly and unjustly. And every one sinning first harms himself, if he harms others; for the evil thing is injurious and harmful, first of all to the one participating in it, harming and damaging him. For the folly of a man defiles his ways, as it is said, 'the foolish will flee from evil' (Prov 14:16). Who is the pit into which the liar, who has done evil, will be cast? For it is written concerning a sinning soul, 'As a pit, so is Sheol' (Ps 183:4), just so.

Its wickedness is a pit. And often in the Scriptures, a pit is taken instead of wickedness, just as when the blind man leads the blind, both shall fall into a pit; and for this reason, blind teachers and students, who are under ignorance and other evils, must be avoided.

46 Having begun from hoping in the Lord his God, the Psalm settles into thanksgiving, as is fitting, having obtained the things requested or faithfully awaiting them; for 'I will confess' (Ps 7:18) declares thanksgiving here; therefore 'I will sing' is joined to it. And he confesses not as if by chance, but according to the righteousness of God; and he sings not aimlessly, but to the name of the Lord the Most High, as he declares having called Him to himself. Therefore also it is high according to holiness and virtue; for no lowly person, but only the one striving for piety, partakes of the Most High's approach.

47 For the life of every man is called a vineyard according to the Scriptures. Concerning such a thing, Naboth the righteous resisted the one demanding tyrannically, choosing rather to die than to give his vineyard to the one who wanted to make it a vegetable garden. For the man is magnanimous and the vineyard is unvanquished, a life most excellent, both practical and contemplative. The wicked desire to take this, not so that it may bear fruit according to its nature, but to tear it down into temporary and quickly withering things, vegetables appropriately named; for he says they will fall quickly like vegetables. This is said concerning those having temporary haste. Near to this vineyard are also those in the 'Aisma' of sins who are named in 'My mother's sons fought against me, they imprisoned me in vineyards; they did not protect my vineyard' (Ps 87:12).' We have passed over this, using only this expression to show for the sake of demonstration what the name of the vineyard signifies: life. He who bears clusters of truth and brings forth grapes through such a vineyard. Since the offspring of the vineyard have a season for being plucked, it is fitting to reap them and bring them into winepresses, so that they might make wine pressing that gladdens the heart of man. And since the life turns out to be both practical and contemplative, the former are the insights of truth, and the latter the work, which is praised for bearing fruit. And it is not one winepress upon which they are brought...

english: Not merely fruits, but more; for the ode is not for a single vintage, but for many vintages. Again, since the practical virtues are many fruits, each will have its own particular vintage; some bear fruits upon the vintage of temperance, those who succeed in chastity and maintain a pure bed; others bear fruits upon the vintage of courage, which those are the farmers of; and concerning the other virtues, they speak of similar things.

Since there are more vintages, those who farm the practical virtues bring them into them like the harvests of vineyards; it is necessary also that those who have borne the clusters of doctrines and theorems of truth bring more into them for the contemplative life. Having said these things, let no one neglect the following of the virtues. For they are one and of the same kind, but since those who partake do not have equal measure toward all, they possess [measure] from which they profit more than others; he who more fully partakes of justice is named from this, and likewise for each of the others. For you will likewise perceive the various beatitudes spoken in the Gospel, one being named from the most powerful grass, another from the merciful, and similarly regarding the rest.

But also in its own number, this ode is composed as the seventy-eighth. For it has much harmony with the resurrection day of the Lord, on which there has become a harvest of many vineyards, as the disciples of the Risen One are sent to make disciples of all nations and to testify to the Risen One to the ends of the earth, so that the proclamation of the Risen One may be spread everywhere, as it is immediately shown from the words of the psalm. 'Great is the name of the Lord in Israel' (Ps 73:2–3), which was said in former times when Israel alone was holding to godliness; but now, the prophecy having been fulfilled, 'all nations shall serve him' (Ps 22:27), (for he is the hope of the nations), 'Wonderful is your name become in all the earth' among those partaking of Christ's proclamation everywhere. For his name has been magnified over all, as it is carried in another psalm. And the cause of his name being wondered at throughout the earth is given in the following verse. For he says, 'Your majesty has been lifted up above the heavens,' so that you...

Having been taken up, rising from the dead, the Christians of the whole earth are called by your designation, O Christ. The majesty of the Savior is being praised; the economy, which received [its purpose] for the salvation of the world, is above the heavens. For what is it to find remaining in it lacking in greatness what is becoming? His majesty was lifted up above the heavens, having been made to sit at the right hand of Majesty in the high places after the cleansing of sins.

By this understanding, it must also be received that he has become higher than the heavens after the resurrection. But let not all those believing from the Gentiles and those coming to the Gospel from the circumcision—who, even if they should ever reach the age of a man, are infants in wickedness, being made infants through simplicity, not knowing evil—[be so]. The difference between infants and sucklings is shown from the word: those receiving milk are sucklings, while those having surpassed this age of infants are being called infants. It is appropriate, as the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians, 'I gave you milk, not food' (1 Cor 3:2). One must watch over this differently: the one being introduced, receiving milk, is a suckling; but the one having been perfected according to understanding, yet being an infant in wickedness, remains an infant. Such are all those having turned and having become like children.

For not much remains to them of having attained the knowledge of you, and of becoming like you in holiness and virtue, to take up as far as is possible (Ps 8:6). But most correctly he said, 'You made him a little lower than [the angels],' but 'You have not made him less [than the angels]' (Ps 8:5). For man, being equal and of equal strength to the immortal rational beings, was made lower than them by the providence of God, through which you alone, the one providing, having been surpassed by mortal life, were struck by the flesh. But even if it has not happened in that way regarding him, he has nonetheless been crowned with surpassing honor and glory by you, because he has become according to your image and likeness, through which image and likeness you have exercised the rational being, having subjected all things to him as being under his feet. english: From here he brings in other words of the psalm. We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, being crowned with glory and honor through the suffering of death; for it was necessary for him, through whom all things and through whom all things, to lead many sons into glory, to perfect the leader of their salvation through sufferings (Ps 8:8–9).

Behold the sequence: it is not set to rule over all mortal creatures, but over the days (Ps 8:10). For the one-horned does not hold sway, nor does he stand against the others, strong and wild, as to rule the days, from the sheep and the ox and all the cattle of the field, and the following. I think this is not well said. For before these transgressions, man ruled; and the righteous rule even after these transgressions, as Daniel, having been thrown into the den of lions and suffering no harm from any of them, and Paul, having shaken off the viper from his own hand upon the fire. For wild beasts, they say, shall make peace with you; and in addition to these, the beasts of the field are included, as we have learned in Genesis.

It is fitting that the song spoken concerning the resurrection of the Savior should have a resemblance to the end at the beginning (Ps 8:10); for beginning and ending use the same words, the Spirit teaching the beginning to be the end according to the subject. It agrees with 'O Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth: let all the earth worship you and sing praises to you' (Ps 9:1).

Since it is not being defined who the Son is, what the Savior is is being made manifest in many ways by being so named. Indeed, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, Paul says, 'Christ, if he is a Son upon his own house, not we are' (Heb 1:8/2:13 context); and again, 'At the end of these days he spoke to us in a Son' (Heb 1:2); and the Savior himself writes about himself in the Gospel, 'If the Son does not set you free, you will be free indeed' (John 8:36). And also the proposed triumphal song has a reference to the end. For on account of that end, the Savior arrived, about which the precursor of the apostles writes: 'Having grasped the end of faith, the salvation of souls, concerning which salvation the prophets searched and inquired, and after a little time, testifying to the sufferings toward Christ...'

Regarding the glories that follow these things. Perhaps the Jews, concerning Absalom as the son of the one singing, will say that the inscription is true, being rebuked as they have not rightly received it, and because they are always in error for not searching the Scriptures. For what is it even plausible to say in the [work] 'On the Hidden Things', if they do not uncover the thoughts of Absalom that occurred in secret, [regarding] how the hidden things lie? And what is said by them possesses much elegance.

Such a sitting signifies him as a judge, but not that a certain seat has been established. Stand firm, if there is room to say, [that] after the nations have been rebuked, the impious shall perish in the manner of their ways, so as to no longer profit them. And this shall happen, the previously spoken thing being fulfilled thus: 'The way of the ungodly shall perish' (Ps 9:7a).

But the aggressions of the enemy are, in a sense, the heretical teachings and the vices according to appearance, which some have left as if they could no longer contend super-abundantly as cities, and they themselves shall be destroyed; for cities are collections of people standing together and being governed unlawfully. For it has been written concerning the one establishing them as 'building cities in vain and preparing cities in iniquity'. For their substance is wrongdoing and the shedding of blood of those being scandalized. The Savior, having arrived, pulls these down, pulling down the enemy who wishes to rule tyrannically, having been as it were cities.

Having seen this courage with divine eyes and speaking well, they say he is the best, as if uttering a gracious voice from one voice, beginning thus: 'Lord my God, I will glorify you, I will praise your name, what you have done wonderful things, an ancient and true counsel'; may it be, Lord, that what you have made cities into dust, a city of the ungodly, shall never be built for ever. Stand firm, if it signifies the raised ruin of Jerusalem, of the Savior having been crucified in it, of its citizens being the remainder of the ungodly because of the killing of the Lord (Ps 9:7b). english: He will fear lest he fall before the one judging in righteousness and uprightness because of false deeds and an impious mindset; for the judgment of him will be inescapable. This is shown by the expression 'at an acceptable time God heard you' (Ps 9:10), and by the first Psalm: 'Arising, you will have mercy on Zion' (Ps 9:11)—what a time to have mercy, what a time that is.

Having ascended above all human confidence (for having knowledge of your name they have secure and perfect trust), they will hope for nothing of those things; but those who want all things from him seek God, wanting to exist not from themselves, and they are not abandoned by him. It is fitting to hear this word piously and wisely. For if anyone thinks that he who prospers in worldly things is not abandoned by God, he errs. For many impious people live thus. It is not to say that Abel was abandoned (for he was slain), but also the prophets and apostles; for they were continually afflicted, and in the end most of them were slain by men. Because of this distinction, we do not say that one held until the last breath is not abandoned by God, even if he suffers myriad times from enemies. For this is truly the not being abandoned by the Lord. The manner in which one must seek God is shown by those having such wisdom: 'Think about the Lord in goodness, and in simplicity of heart seek him, who is found by those not testing him, but is revealed to those not being unfaithful to him' (Ps 9:12–13).

Those who have practiced singing with spirit and mind are commanded to sing a hymn, but they do not sing thus with pious understanding and thought of the spirit; for they are commanded to sing even dreadfully and to sing with the heart. Those who do not sing thus to the Lord dwelling in Zion according to the guidance of the Holy Spirit receive another command toward him in the...

To announce to the nations his excellencies. These are, namely, what he marvelously did having arrived, both intelligible and sensible things. And the second command is said especially to the apostles having been sent, to disciple all the nations. And what they seek, their souls remembered those having been snatched away by the fiery arrows of the evil one.

By these, he says, the 'He did not forget the cry of the poor' is applied, so that no one will be at a loss saying: how did the poor from the nations cry to God, even though having been snatched away by the prevailing many-minded deception and by the invisible enemies working it? It must truly be said to bring up their cry, just as the blood of Abel cries to God and the reward having been deprived of the workers; for he says, 'Behold, the reward of those who have not sown your lands cries out, that which has been deprived from you' (Ps 9:13).

And another understanding is said; not entirely the same as those from the nations, of whom the souls remembered, the poor are those of whom the benefactor did not forget the voice. For they are not able to be those concerning the nations having prophetically pre-announced, of whom one says, 'Those from the ends of the earth' (Ps 72:32) and the other, 'All the nations, all that you have done, shall worship before you' (Ps 86:9). And the poor are also in these, it is said, those lacking much of the wealth of divinity and of the divine knowledge; for they were partially prophesying in the end.

Regarding that one being below death, it is not written, 'Death swallowed up by strength' (Ps 88:4); the enemies make those being humbled by it to become, either through maltreatment or through sinning. From this death and from the humbling upon it, it is possible to be outside by the mercy of God. english: The awareness of one's own evils and the knowledge of God's goodness leads to the prayer, 'Have mercy on me and see the humiliation that has come upon me from my enemies' (Ps 9:15b). For they humiliated me by dragging me down; but You alone are able to lift me up from the gates of death through a goodness that is essentially present.

Regarding the daughters of Zion, those participating in this must hear in harmony with being called sons of light, peace, and wisdom. The gates of the daughter of Zion, being opposite the gates of death, are praiseworthy deeds and contemplations of God's virtue and wisdom to be fulfilled.

Concerning the incorruptible virtue, it is said: 'The grace [is] with those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption' (Ps 9:16), while the opposite, evil, will be called corruption and destruction. It is shown that corruption is called evil from the saying, 'If anyone destroys the temple of God' (1 Cor 3:17), and from what is said to the wicked in the prophet, 'Because of incorruption you have been corrupted by destruction.' This is consistent with, 'Who will help you against your corruption, O Israel?' (Hos 4:9). The corruption so spoken of, in the doing of what is, is promised to be accomplished by those who possess it. The word says that the mortals have fallen into that in which they practiced corruption (Ps 7:15). For no one else is seized by another's impiety and sin; for each one dies by his own sin.

And since the wicked, having first harmed themselves and others through deceit, attempt to bring the same harm by trial, they secretly prepare snares in their treacherous wisdoms and words to catch the unsuspecting. By that very snare they are punished. For they render justice and through those whom they deceived. And to suffer thus becomes a judgment of the provident God; for how is it not His judgment that, in His works, He seizes the sinner who has used the pretext of acting wickedly to be condemned from without? This is consistent with what was said a little earlier: 'He who digs a pit will fall into it' (Ps 7:15). Having spoken about the psalm of lament, the song of the lament must now be spoken. Having begun the present psalm from 'I will confess to You, Lord,' the proclamation extended as 'The sinner was caught'; after which the words of the song [begin]...

Since 'Let the sinners be turned away' follows the interlude, the name of the hymn is entwined with the interlude. For if the whole psalm is called a hymn, the preface of the hymn was always arranged in a way and with a power before it, as is demonstrated for many psalms. But since it is not so here, and since the beginning is taken after the interlude, it is fitting that 'Hymn of the interlude' be placed in between. It will be shown how the hymn possesses the thought of the following, with their words being set forth: 'Let the sinners be turned away' etc. Ps 9:18–19: 'Let the sinners be turned away, those imposing judgment against the righteous, into the abyss.'

Interpreting who the sinners are, he brought forward that the things being forgotten are mortal things of God. But sinners and mortals must be understood not as men only, but also as fleshless powers. For if the sinner does not signify essence, but rather what kind of voice the sinner is—a nickname not from the sin itself—then everyone participating in sin would not be called thus. Appropriately to these things, the mortals will also be called. Just as one who is not locally in heaven, but walking upon the earth, is able to possess citizenship and thought there, so also one not dwelling locally in the abyss is able to bear signs of death and of sinning himself, as if he dwells in the abyss, even though he is among those in the life after the body.

And he is called poor, the one impoverishing through sin, and the moderate and the foolish, and the one needing to receive from God; and such a one is born wretched. According to all these ways, the one called poor is remembered by God. For through something advantageous, some forgetfulness of him might occur, but it does not remain entirely so, and for this reason he will not be forgotten unto the end. As for who will be judged poor or needy, we will say as the opportunity calls us to speak about these things. Ps 9:20: 'You, Lord, make those who stagger and those who faint fall from the lofty height, opposing the proud; let them not then be strong, but let them be judged before you; for a surpassing benefit will spring forth for them.'

Πλὴν εἰ καὶ πολλὴ ἡ θησαυρισθεῖσα ὑπ' αὐτοῦ ὀργή, ἀλλά γε οὐκ ε σται κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος καὶ μέγεθος αὐτῆς ἐκζήτησις ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως δι' ἀγαθότητα τοῦ κρίνοντος θεοῦ. εἰ γὰρ ἐκζήτησις κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῆς ὀργῆς ἐγίνετο, α ρδην ἀπώλλυντο καὶ παρ' αὐτὰ οἱ κακοί. τοῦτ' αὐτὸ θεωρήσαντες τῷ ἀγαθότητα ἐνδεικνυμένῳ φασὶν ̓Εὰν ἀνομίας παρατηρήσῃ, κύριε, κύριε, τίς ὑποστήσεται; Πρόφασις δὲ τοῦ παροξύναι τὸν ἁμαρτωλὸν τὸν κύριόν ἐστιν τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν καὶ ἐνώπιον αὐτὸν ε χειν, ἐπείπερ ἀπεστράφη θεόν. πᾶς γὰρ ἁμαρτάνων τοῦτο πράττει· διό φησιν ὁ θεὸς περὶ παντὸς τοιούτου Εστρεψαν ἐπ' ἐμὲ νῶτα αὐτῶν καὶ οὐχὶ πρόσωπα. ταύτης τῆς ἀσεβείας ὁ Κάϊν πατὴρ γεγονὼς ̓Εξῆλθεν ἀπὸ προσώπου κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ ἀποστραφεὶς αὐτὸν δηλονότι. Εἰ περὶ ἀνθρώπων ἁμαρτωλῶν λέγεται ταῦτα, πολλῷ μᾶλλον καὶ περὶ διαβόλου παροξύναντος τὸν θεὸν καὶ οὐκ ε χοντος αὐτὸν ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ. μάλιστα γὰρ αἱ ἑπόμεναι λέξεις περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγονται· Βεβηλοῦνται αἱ ὁδοὶ αὐτοῦ ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ. τίνος γὰρ ἀνθρώπου Βεβηλοῦνται αἱ ὁδοὶ ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ, τῶν ἀσεβῶν καθηκόντως πολλὰ πολλάκις ἐπιτελούντων; βαδίζει δὲ βεβήλως οὐκ εἰς μόνας πράξεις ἐπιλήπτους α γων τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπρονοησίαν ὁρίζων. πολλοὺς γοῦν ε πεισεν ἀπροστασίαστον τὸν κόσμον δογματίσαι, πρότερον αὐτὸς ἐκπεσὼν τῆς ὀρθῆς περὶ διοικήσεως θεοῦ καὶ κρίσεως γνώμης. παρίσταται τοῦτο ἐκ τοῦ λεγομένου τῷ θεῷ περὶ αὐτοῦ ̓Ανταναιρεῖται τὰ κρίματά σου ἀπὸ προσώπου αὐτοῦ, πάντων τῶν ἐχθρῶν αὐτοῦ κατακυριεύσει, οὐχ ὡς πάντως τοῦτο σχήσοντος, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν τοῦτο προτεθεῖσθαι· ψεῦδος γὰρ τὸ
english: I will take the inhabited world in my hand as a disease and as abandoned dust to wipe away; no one shall escape me or answer me.

The human race does not bring the words of its pride as an embassy to the Savior, saying, 'Arise, O Lord, descend to us, so that the human who is proud against us may not be strengthened for long.' For the devil says that 'man' is not a mortal rational animal, but that they have fallen away from divinity just as those to whom God said, 'I am; you are gods and all are sons of the Most High, but you, as men, die' (Ps 82:6).

The prophet asks like a man and inquires of God, saying, 'Why, Lord, have you stood far off?' (Ps 22:13). If the Word responds to him, what is the good of God for the repentance of sinners? For God has stood far from the sinners, His presence discerning the sin itself and driving the sinners far away according to what has been said: 'Your sins divide [you] between me and you' (Ps 83:15). Otherwise, God is always present to all and happens to fill all things everywhere. Therefore it has been said in the prophecies: 'I am a God approaching,' says the Lord, 'and not a God from afar.'

But for the righteous who are afflicted in the present life and oppressed by the ungodly, he says, 'As if standing far off, you abandon them, O Lord, and look down from above' (Ps 22:14). Consequently, the pride of the ungodly increases, while He burns your poor and wretched one, the God-fearing man, who zealously desires and inwardly burns the soul with zeal.

And especially those who are deprived of divine wealth and wisdom and are not precise concerning the doctrines of piety; for they do not stumble upon judgments praising the sinner for that which he desires, it being manifest that the sinner reaches out not for the heretical but for the pleasant and the passionate. Along with these, they consider wealth and human, fleeting glory to be a blessing from the same error, asserting that the wrongdoers are blessed by God; but it is necessary to examine how the blessing of God is given to the righteous.
Even if it has seemed that God stands far off and looks down from above on the afflicted because of being troubled by the pride of the ungodly...

But he does not very much rage against the proud one having stumbled and, if it is said according to the scripture, having set fire to the poor man because of the bad use of the things that were to him by God's providence. For this is shown from the following words: for it is said, 'The sinner provoked the Lord.' And the one provoking is the impious one, praising himself according to his own desires. And he provoked the Lord to such an extent as for the anger to become stretched out, that he himself has stored up for himself according to what was said, 'According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up for yourself wrath in a day of wrath' (Ps 7:16).

However, even if much wrath has been stored up by him, nevertheless there will not be a search according to the abundance and greatness of it on the day of judgment because of the goodness of the judging God. For if a search according to the abundance of the wrath were to happen, the wicked would immediately be lost. Having seen this very thing, they say, regarding the goodness being shown: 'If iniquity is observed, Lord, Lord, who will endure?' (Ps 53:2). The pretext for the sinner provoking the Lord is not having him before the eyes and in the presence, since he has turned away from God. For every one sinning does this; therefore God says concerning every such one, 'They turned their backs on me, and not faces' (Ps 53:2).

Cain, having become the father of this impiety, 'Went out from the presence of the Lord God, having turned away from him' (Gen 4:16) clearly. If these things are said concerning sinful men, much more concerning the devil, having provoked God and not having him before him. For especially the following words are said concerning him: 'His ways are defiled at all times' (Ps 106:18). For whose ways are defiled at all times, except of the impious, habitually performing many, many things? And he walks impiously, not only in single acts seizing men, but also defining unprovidence.

Indeed, he has persuaded many to dogmatize the unprotected world, having first himself fallen from the right opinion concerning God's administration and judgment. This is shown from what is said to God concerning him, 'Your judgments are overthrown from his face; he shall lord it over all his enemies' (Ps 72:4), not as if he were going to do this always, but because this very thing is set forth; for it is a lie...

english: He will be Lord over all his enemies. For especially his enemies are those perfect in holiness in whom no one rules. But he rules over only those practicing sin; for it is said, 'Everyone practicing sin is a slave to sin.' And the slave of sin is ruled over by the devil, who has worked sin in him. And according to the insatiable nature of his wickedness, what follows is brought forth: 'For if indeed,' he says, 'I shall never be shaken from generation to generation by evil' (Ps 9:28). The word reveals his arrogance together with impudence. By this voice, one having understood will interpret regarding only those humans who have become his enemies, to say that he will rule over all his enemies. For if indeed from generation to generation one has never been shaken in heart by evil, it is evident that the saying refers only to humans having the 'being' in succession. But even this is not entirely true; for he did not rule over the holy patriarchs and prophets and apostles; rather, they themselves stretched out this authority under the feet of Jesus.

He, having fallen away from his holiness, truth, and blessing, leading himself far away, has a mouth full of curses, through which he says, testing, making a punishment and a curse upon those being deceived. And his word has much wickedness along with the harm; therefore, along with the curse and bitterness and deceit, his word is full, being called his mouth. And since he brings forth none of these things to harm and destroy under his tongue, but the word itself is harmful, pain and toil exist; for nothing is gentle or kind, but if he brings in toil and pain, he brings it forth.

Setting before himself harm and destruction through all things, he chooses men appearing to be rich in word (having pseudonymous knowledge), and sitting with them, he tries to sit hidden so as to remain unknown, to kill the innocent by wounding him with his burning arrows (Ps 9:29-32); for these are things scattering death, striking the one being cast from the life with virtue by the arrows. It is possible to pierce and thus: 'He sits in a seat with...'

Of the rich; with the stichoi we bring forward 'To kill the innocent in secret.' For the 'in secret' part causes doubt, being divided in two ways, as we have previously noted by stichoi: 'He sits in the seat with the rich in secret' (Ps 2:6), [followed by] 'to kill the innocent.' However, even if he sits in a seat with the aforementioned rich, intending to look and to kill the innocent, it is necessary to oversee that no one of the God-wise may be able to wound one clothed in the panoply of God; for he, obeying the command to turn his eyes toward the poor man, has him captured, the same one acting toward the poor man being scorched by the impiety of the ungodly's pride.

He sits in secret, a fierce lion in his den, to snatch the poor man through deceptive words (and indeed also through deeds), and he will drag him after snatching him into his trap in order to devour him. For he is a fierce beast, rather even a lion. Often indeed, sitting in a seat and seemingly speaking about stewardship, he conceals the matter concerning love of money. As one speaking about temperance, he proposes a manner of intemperance, just as the serpent deceived Eve in the paradise through the transgression of the commandment, setting up equality, and likewise Judas through love of money. The 'looking down' written there shows that, having turned the eye downward, he fell; for how could he not direct his gaze downward, he who rejects Providence, by saying 'God has forgotten' and the following things? (Ps 9:35–37a)

Being able immediately to humble the proud one who tyrannizes those being shaken by his audacity, for what is the use, being able to help them, if you allow them a certain time to be afflicted, during which you understood not only the pain upon him and through him? And this has happened, so that those who have benefited through the timely affliction may willingly deliver themselves into your hands, having a remaining desire to be disciplined and to be ruled by you. To you, then, the poor man is not abandoned; you will manage the things concerning his salvation, so that you may make him rich by providing good things from heaven. So also he helps the orphan, presiding over and rearing him into the rank of a son. An orphan in these things...

english: The devil, who once had a father through wickedness, must now be cast out by a manner of repentance. The symbols of these received orphans seeking help by God are Abraham leaving his father's house to follow God when called, and the sons of Zebedee leaving their father after the exhortation of Jesus saying, 'Follow me.'

But who is the sinner and evil, as spoken of with the article, the devil? His arm is broken by the Lord, and his sin, being sought, is not found, having found its end in its fulfillment. For evil is not a certain substance but a quality, and thus the end will be established over all things, not because all other things have become so; for he himself is nothing, as there is no end to his kingdom. For one cannot be under two lords and kings. The one who ruled and reigned was the sin of the one doing it; God is not the lord or king of the one sinning. And since the sin that was ruling the one acting it was sought, it was not found, the Lord reigns forever and unto the age of ages.

It is said of the good heart of the earth of God (Ps 9:37). From this earth mortals perish, if every vain thought and evil purpose is cast out; for vain thoughts and purposes are mortal, being destroyed by the blessing of God. But if someone wishes to signify even the land of the gentle (for it also belongs to the Lord), mortals perish from this earth. For no one sinning is permitted to ascend into it; for only the saints shall inherit it. For it is said to someone holy: 'I believe to see the good things of the Lord among the living in the land' (Ps 9:38). And to another God says: 'I will bring you up to the good things of the earth' (Ps 9:38).
The desire of the poor was to see the one who tyrannically ruled over them fall. Since he has not risen...

Because the desire of the sinful and evil man is worn away at the arm, it is fitting that it is revealed to God, who oversees hearts and knows the hidden thing, as an active prayer. But the Lord heard them, paying attention with his ear to the readiness of their ruling principle; for how would the heart not be ready toward salvation, those having desire for the things foretold? (Ps 9:39).

In this way, the man must be caught out, either by boasting toward the mortal rational animal, or toward the one saying, 'I will seize the world with my hand, and no one shall escape me or answer me, the deceiver.' For he will not magnify himself while being crushed under the feet of the saints who tread upon his power, Jesus, this [one] having granted. (Ps 10:1-2).

And it should be read also thus: 'In the Lord I have trusted'; how do you say to my soul, 'Behold, the sinners have bent a bow, they have prepared arrows in a quiver,' and the following? (Ps 10:1-2). Upon these spoken things, the soul is urged to be poised like a sparrow with the wings of virtue, so that having passed over the high mountains, it might remain harmless among the spiritual things. And how one should bear the distinctions of the reading, it is fitting to trust in the Lord. (Ps 10:1-2).

According to theory: as if the ruling principle were held ready against many sophistically prepared visible and invisible enemies, resembling a bow drawn in readiness, and also arrows prepared, and persuasive words [are used]; in order that you might shoot down [the enemy], you have a passage through high mountains, and having occurred there, you will not be harmed. It is said that the more divine meanings of the Scriptures are signified by the correspondence of the things seen; toward these, also the wise teachers, apostles, and prophets. It is possible through the Spirit to grasp the saying, 'Repent, go to the mountains like a sparrow,' exhorting one to withdraw, desiring to run from the venomous strike of the archers. And if even invisible powers [are]...

english: The relatives of the archers should not say 'Repent like a sparrow' in a mocking way, which we shall reject, wanting to show those who trust in God with a whole heart.

Since the archers prepared to sophistize are sons of darkness and of night, those having a straight heart set themselves to shoot in the clear night. [Ps 10:3b] The Lord is righteous; what will he do? Will he lay snares upon the sinners and divide to them a cup of punishment, so that while drinking them they become weak from the impulse to shoot? [Ps 10:4-7] Concerning the Father, and also Him, the Savior: before the incarnation, His holy temple was to be rejected, having the holy and heavenly thought concerning Him. [Ps 10:4] In His holy temple and He has the throne in heaven, reigning divinely and supernaturally. We also noted that previously the throne was taken instead of the kingdom.

But the watchful ones and the powers of God, called His eyes, become toward the sufferer, guarding him harmless from those appointed around him. The eyelids of the eyes of God examine the actions and the thoughts of men. From this, the philanthropy of the Judge is shown. For if He examined with eyes and not with eyelids, the judgment would be unendurable to men. But His examining with His own eyelids does not mean all the sins of those judged are observed, nor do these exist in magnitude.

It is also possible to say: His eyes are upon the one being benefited, if a sufferer exists, but the eyelids are upon the sons; many men's sons, if the benefits are abundantly and boldly accomplished, but the punishments hide much concerning God. And these things he will say by thought; they show no perceptible eyelid or anything of that kind, therefore these things must be thought of in a God-befitting way. Christ is not to be revealed on a step; all must be brought to each one what he has done through the body, whether good or evil. Having said this, under the Lord's examination being done of the righteous and the ungodly, he brings it as if he hates his own soul, the one doing evil without hating it as injustice, making it subject to punishment because of sinning; he acts contrary to the one acting justly.

He who loves his soul and his neighbor as himself strives toward virtue. The Lord does not fight, but examines the righteous and the impious by the fact that the impious do not stand up in judgment. For the former signifies those who are entirely atheistic, while the latter signifies those who despise God because of sinning. For the Scriptures declare this, especially that which says, 'The righteous shall be like the impious' in Genesis.

He will lay snares upon sinners, that is, he will punish them by making snares and by keeping those being hunted within them, unless they are delivered up by him to the desires of their own hearts; this is also declared by the sufferings of dishonor and an unproven mind. And therefore, if not for this, it is said 'He will lay snares' rather than 'He will rain snares'; for those having been ensnared by themselves are being rained upon with snares. This is also declared from 'The Lord will lead those turning into straits with those working iniquity.'

You will apply to the latter the recompenses, as it is written in Proverbs: 'God sends toward crooked, crooked ways.' Regarding the former recompense, you will punish by sending crooked ways to those who have become crooked through wickedness; but regarding the latter, the recompenses are those being delivered up, which are shown through the sufferings of dishonor and those being reproached. 'Fire and sulfur and a spirit of tempest are the portion of their cup.'

The painful recompenses are often declared in the Scripture by the name of the cup, as in Isaiah: 'Arise, arise, Jerusalem, pouring out the cup of downfall, the bowl of your fury,' and the following; but also in Jeremiah the same is presented from the sound of that voice: 'Take the cup of the wrath of my uncontrolled anger from my hand, and you shall make all the nations drink it, whom I have sent against you.' Does not this also signify the punishment in the things set forth by the portion of the cup divided to them, especially what the fullness of this cup is: 'Fire and sulfur and a spirit of tempest'? The things written in Genesis are not symbols, if they are the punishments having come upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord; toward this fire and sulfur and spirit of tempest is the watering of the cup. english: It is a threat of burning, but the divine thing that awakens is rather the fire as a starting point. Along with these, the Spirit indicates a turning of some kind of storm of temptation. And as to what kind of temptation the storm indicates, it is clearly to be learned from that which is written in Isaiah: 'As a storm passing through the desert, coming near, its appearance is fearful and its hardness was announced to me.' Let us therefore flee from impiety, so that this cup may be far from us, and let us live in piety, so that we may drink the intoxicating cup as strongest; for perhaps even that is said: 'The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.'

For the Lord is just and loved justice, and straightness is his face. For this reason, he watches his eyes over the poor for his salvation, but also upon the sinners he sends snares. For it does not happen by chance, if it becomes of the providence and the judgment of God; for the Lord is just in essence, not merely in participation of justice. Moreover, even if he does not have it by nature, he does not love the justices that are in the many righteous, accepting the intention of each. It is also possible to say another way that he loves justices; since there is justice in the judgment of each, and the judgments of God are many, about which it is written: 'The judgments of the Lord are true and justified'; on the same basis, it is necessary that many justices also exist. And as he is just, so also seeing straightness; and straightness you say is the opinion being regulated toward the right reason; he sees this rejoicing in those who have it. It may also be said regarding straightness in harmony with the second thought concerning the justiceses existing in his unsearchable judgments, which he sees because of the utterly accepting of his face; for God appears present in the works of providence and in the results of the judgments.

As the fullness of the deceit and wickedness of humanity, as if there were no mercy and truth and knowledge of God on the earth, there has become a need for the arrival of the Savior toward us, for the destruction of the existing harm (Ps 11:1). To this end that which is in Jeremiah shall take place: 'Each will play with his neighbor, they will not speak truth; their tongue has learned to speak lies' (Ps 11:2). Why is it not 'the truth' but 'the truths'? The one [reason] is because of the...

The various impieties in transactions, and the wrong opinions in dogmas. For it is not necessary to consider the members of the body being destroyed, but their deceitful use and their boastful speech; for even in Proverbs it is said: 'Remove from yourself a crooked mouth and long deceitful lips from you' (Prov 20:14). Our lips are with us; who is our master? From this audacity the impious man, prospering in finding what he desires, utters a voice like that in Job (Job 10:2): 'Depart from me, I do not wish to know your ways; what is sufficient, what shall we serve him?' For indeed they do not think the prosperity coming to them is due to anything, saying to the Lord: 'Depart; do not make your ways manifest to me; for I do not wish to know them; for what more is of us sufficient, that we may serve you?'

Regarding the impious ones thinking much of themselves as having a boastful tongue and deceitful lips, the poor suffer and the needy groan, not bearing their tyranny (Ps 11:6). Therefore the Lord says: 'I will arise now, having placed my counsel in salvation; I will speak boldly in it against those swelling up proudly of the lowly; and I will release the poor and the needy from suffering and groaning.' You say 'the poor' and in this also 'the needy' to exhort themselves through the weakness coming to them or through the wickedness leading to such a state. Indeed, they have not become superior to suffering and groaning, because the Lord, at the time of the visitation, has arisen and has come to us so that the salvation of those who have suffered and groaned might be made manifest. It is indeed appropriate to hear the following: 'I am a wretched man; who will rescue me from this body of death?' (Rom 7:24). Upon which, speaking boldly thereafter, he says: 'I thank God through Jesus Christ.' For it is shown through these things how Jesus Christ, who rescued the wretched one from the body of death, is the one who said: 'I will arise now,' says the Lord.
